body.heading: Find your pinecone
paragraphs: Look on the ground under a pine tree for a dry, open pinecone. Your adult can tie a string to the top so you can hang it near a door or window.
Pinecones are not just decorations. They hold the tree's seeds, and they can move all by themselves — very, very slowly.

body.heading: Watch it change
paragraphs: On a dry, sunny day, look at your pinecone. Its scales spread wide open. On a wet, rainy day, look again. The scales close up tight.
The cone closes when the air is wet to keep its seeds dry and safe. When the air dries, it opens again to let the seeds fly away.

body.heading: Be a weather watcher
paragraphs: Check your pinecone every morning. Draw what it looks like in your notebook and write down the weather too.
Soon you may spot the pattern before you even look out of the window. Your pinecone is a tiny weather station.

takeaway: A pinecone opens in dry air and closes in wet air, so it can tell you about the weather.
safetyNotes: Only pick up pinecones from the ground. Wash your hands after handling things from outdoors.
screenFreeExtension: Keep a pinecone weather diary for a week and draw the cone each day next to the real weather.
